title: Better and Saner Grading Tip: Stop “Relaxing” While Grading
author: Stuart Jr., Dave
summary: Stuart argues that the common habit of grading student writing while watching television is a false economy. Grading is active mental work, and pairing it with a show forces the brain to switch constantly, as if one tried to jog while reading a book. The result is less enjoyment of the show and less productive grading than two exclusive half-hour blocks would give. He cites Daniel Willingham's research summary that mentally challenging tasks should be done on their own. He worries that the habit may over time erode the ability to engage deeply for sustained periods. His rule is to relax when it is time to relax and to be done when work is done, which makes this a piece about teacher work habits and wellbeing.
points: Grading is active mental work, so doing it alongside a TV show degrades both the work and the rest.
The jogging-while-reading analogy shows why task-switching costs quality and time.
Willingham is cited for the research claim that challenging tasks should be done on their own.
Stuart suspects long-term damage to the capacity for sustained deep work, and recommends single-tasking.
quotes: But here is the problem: grading and/or giving feedback on student writing is active, mental work. Trying to grade while watching Netflix is akin to trying to jog while visually reading a book.
So you're sitting here, forcing your brain to try constantly switching between engaging with the show or engaging with the grading task.

After an hour of this, you end up, again, with probably much less enjoyment from the show and much less productivity with the grading than you could have gotten by giving an exclusive 30 minutes to each.
The literature is clear on this point. Engaging in any mentally challenging task should be done on its own — not while also watching television or carrying on a conversation.

At best, they decrease the quality of our evenings and increase the amount of time it takes to complete tasks. At worst, I wouldn't be surprised if we're damaging our brains, decreasing our ability over time to deeply engage with mentally challenging work for periods of, say, 60 minutes at a time.
When it's time to relax, relax. - When it's time to be done working, be done working.
